title: Fergus and the Quiet Place
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks of the Whisperwind Archipelago were not known for silence. Far from it. The wind, a constant companion, scurried and chattered between soaring cloud-kissed peaks. Nestled at the foot of the highest, in a sturdy stone cottage that gleamed with tidy pride, lived Fergus. Not the noisy club-waving sort of ogre. A gentle, steady giant. Hands as large as baking sheets, with a master clockmaker’s delicate touch. A heart as big and calm as a mountain lake. With him, always, Parsnip: a goat whose fleece shimmered like pale morning mist, bright intelligent eyes holding a spark of quiet knowing. My quiet friend, Fergus called him, which was as close to a vow as an ogre needed.

Fergus woke with a rumble like distant thunder. Parsnip was already at work, grooming the ogre’s beard with a surprisingly skilful horn, as if a tidy beard were the first duty of a quiet morning. “A quiet day, Parsnip. Just a quiet, peaceful day.” He had said it aloud. That, as any creature who has wished for peace knows, can be the first mistake. The kettle had not even sung. The cottage still smelled of yesterday’s thyme.

No sooner had he stepped outside than Old Man Hemlock beamed, spectacles polished to a blinding sheen. “Ah, Fergus, the very ogre. The bridge across the Gurgling Gorge has a loose plank. With your magnificent strength you could pop over and tighten it. Neatest plan. Quick and tidy, like a well-stitched seam.”

“Neat, perhaps,” Fergus said, voice a low warm rumble. “A trifle exposed to the wind. And the currents under the gorge. A stronger gust and that plank might drift among the Cloud Meadows. A different approach might be wiser. One that takes the mountain’s breath into account.”

Before Hemlock could ponder mountain breaths, Mayor Gable bustled up, flushed with importance. “The Sky-Ferry rope across the Great Chasm is fraying. Sunpetal seeds must reach market. You stand on one side and tie a new rope across. So obvious it is brilliant.”

Fergus had been about to suggest weaving Whispering Woods vines into the existing rope, a steadier, less dramatic job. A furrow appeared. “Clever, Mayor? Or a touch ambitious? Imagine the swing if the wind catches it. We cannot possibly panic yet. We have not even had our mid-morning tea.”

Parsnip nudged his hand. A soft maa. My quiet friend, agreeing. Fergus packed no rope. He packed no plank. He packed a small tin of tea leaves and a patience that did not like being volunteered.

They ambled a less-travelled pass, winding between two particularly grumpy-looking cloud-shrouded peaks. The air grew cooler. The wind’s usual noisy chatter softened to a mere whisper, as if the mountains themselves were sharing secrets. They passed a patch of shimmering Moonmoss, pearly light on the rocky path. A true sense of peace, like dew settling on a spider’s web, began to embrace Fergus. Parsnip walked close, fleece brushing an enormous knuckle. My quiet friend, keeping pace.

Pebbles skittered, not dangerous, but enough to block the path. Fergus sighed, ready to clear them with enormous hands, when Parsnip scrambled up an outcrop and nudged a medium boulder. It tumbled, pushed the scatter aside, and opened the way with a satisfying rumble. Fergus’s smile was slow. “Well done. A most efficient, and certainly quiet, solution.”

Deeper still they discovered a cave mouth almost hidden by a curtain of cascading verdant ferns. Soft radiant gold spilled out, illuminating rock and reflecting in a small perfectly still mountain pool. The water became liquid sunshine, shimmering and inviting. Utterly beautiful. A perfect place for rest.

“Ah,” Fergus breathed, sinking onto moss, the day’s well-meaning plans melting. “This is precisely what I sought.” He closed his eyes, ready to doze, when a low grumbling came from the depths.

A low grumble. From the cave came a creature the colour of gathering storm clouds, eyes like dull unpolished pebbles: a Grumble-Grumble, territorial and perpetually dissatisfied.

“Who’s disturbing the peace? This is my sun-warmed resting spot.”

“We meant no intrusion. We sought repose. The light is most inviting.”

The Grumble-Grumble puffed. “It’s mine. You have the neatest plan to steal it.”

Fergus saw it then. The creature was not angry about light. It was worried about being alone. Countless solitary afternoons in that gold, fearing company meant being forgotten. “Your plan was to enjoy it. Ours was to share the warmth. Perhaps we can find a compromise.”

The Grumble-Grumble kept glancing at Parsnip, wary, almost curious. “Parsnip is an excellent listener. He makes the quietest places feel less empty. While we rest, he can keep you company. Less disruptive than you assume.”

They sat. For a stretch nobody spoke. Gold on water. Parsnip chewed sweet grass with a low contented hum, a vibration that seemed to soothe the rough edges of the Grumble-Grumble’s temper. The stormy fur eased. A rumbling sigh, more resignation than anger, and it settled, observing with hesitant interest. Silent perseverance: three creatures sharing a pool and not inventing a better plan. The ferns at the cave mouth dripped. A dragonfly sketched a slow circle and left.

Fergus had not been volunteered for ropes or planks. He had observed, listened, and let my quiet friend do the introducing. The gold warmed his face like a held cup. Parsnip’s chewing was a lullaby. The Grumble-Grumble’s pebble eyes stayed open, but they were no longer counting trespassers.

Sun went down in rose and amethyst. Parsnip curled by Fergus’s enormous foot. The Grumble-Grumble kept the cave and the company both. Hemlock’s plank and Gable’s rope would wait until after tea, which, Fergus thought, was the mountain’s preferred schedule. He did not make a speech about quiet being the most valuable thing. He poured the tin at last, steam lifting into gold, and the pool held its sunshine a little longer than the sky, and that was enough of a reign.
characters: Fergus (gentle ogre), Parsnip (a goat of quiet knowing)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
